catalog_quote: Contour units are penultimately stressed or finally stressed. (Garvin 1948:37)
sweep_summary: Kutenai (kute1249) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant on a second-hand StressTyp2 quotation of Garvin 1948:37 ('penultimately stressed or finally stressed'). The only title-keyword item, McClay 2017 'Focus in Ktunaxa: word order and prosody' (UBC MA thesis), is a focus-prosody study; its abstract (DataCite, saved) reports that foci are louder and higher-pitched and says nothing about word-stress placement; the full text is behind UBC's browser-verification wall by automated download and direct download (2026-09-16 and 09-17), with no the Internet Archive, OATD, BASE, CORE, LAC or search-engine route open today — medium priority to obtain via a browser/a Harvard login. this search of works with stress in the title instead downloaded the open eScholarship scan of Morgan 1991 (the catalog's own grammar, previously cited only second-hand) and scanned its stress pages: §2.5.3 p.114 states one Penultimate Stress Assignment rule giving phrasal stress on the phrase penult and weaker word stress on each word's penult, plus rhythmical alternating stress; fn.3 p.112 confines final stress to French loans, Christian names, a very few native words and one Garvin phrase. This is a first-hand statement that confirms the fixed-dominant (penultimate) coding and refines the 'or finally stressed' clause to marginal exceptions; it should replace the StressTyp2 paraphrase as the deciding source. Garvin 1948 itself remains paywalled (UChicago DOI 403; online with a university library loginexists).

new_statements.quote: There is one strictly mid-level stress assignment rule, Penultimate Stress Assignment. It is responsible for full (phrasal) stress on the penultimate phonemic vowel (or on the only phonemic vowel) of every phrase. This same rule is also responsible for instances of word stress, not as strong as full phrasal stress, which occur on the penultimate phonemic vowel (or on the only phonemic vowel) of individual words in a phrase, at least where there is no conflict with full phrasal stress. There is also some evidence for a rule of Rhythmical Stress Assignment which assigns still weaker instances of stress to every second syllable of a phrase
new_statements.citation: Morgan, Lawrence R. 1991. A Description of the Kutenai Language. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley, §2.5.3 'The Stress Assignment Rules', p. 114 (eScholarship open-access scan, p. 138; read via tesseract scanned at 200 dpi)
new_statements.reading: Kutenai word stress is fixed penultimate (penultimate phonemic vowel of each word; monosyllables stressed on their only vowel), with a stronger penultimate PHRASAL stress that overrides clashing word stresses and a weaker alternating rhythmical stress counting leftward from the phrasal penult. Final stress is confined to exceptions: French loans, most Christian names, 'a very few' native words such as /taxta'/ 'later', and one phrase-final case quoted from Garvin 1948a p.38 (fn. 3, p. 112). This supports the catalog's fixed-dominant (penultimate) coding and narrows StressTyp2's 'penultimately stressed or finally stressed' (Garvin 1948:37) to penultimate-dominant with marginal final exceptions; Morgan states (p.114) that Garvin's facts 'are in line with the facts as reported here' once phrasal, word and rhythmical stress are distinguished. (scanned rendered 'rule' as 'tule' twice; corrected in the quote.)

new_statements.quote: the autosegmental metrical theory of intonational phonology (Ladd 2008, i.a.), maps prosodic components (pitch accents, lengthening, and stress) onto phonological components (syllables and words). The key findings are as follows: 1. Ktunaxa answers have a default word order of Subject-Verb-Object, contrary to patterns emerging in texts; 2. Word order changes relative to the type of question asked: foci are slightly more likely to be sentence-initial; 3. Ktunaxa employs prosody to mark focus in answers: foci are louder and higher in pitch; 4. Some focus-sensitive operators also trigger prosodic cues in their associates. Further work is needed to fully describe Ktunaxa prosody

new_statements.quote: 1.3.2 Phonetics and phonology of Ktunaxa. The facts of Ktunaxa phonology that are most relevant to this thesis have to do with the nature of stress and pitch-bearing units (vowels and other sonorants). Based on findings from previous work, I assume that there are word “contours” with final or penultimate stress (Garvin, 1948c, p. 37). The definition of a ‘contour’ is comparable to that of a phonological word; the present analysis does not explore the intonational phonology of Ktunaxa to the point of describing different levels of phonological phrasing in the language, so this assumption is left as it stands. Two correlates of word- (or phrase-) level stress in Ktunaxa are pitch and intensity, which are higher in stressed syllables than unstressed ones (Morgan, 1991, p. 77).

new_statements.relation_note: Restates the catalog's own deciding sentence (StressTyp2 < Garvin 1948:37 'penultimately stressed or finally stressed') and defers to Morgan 1991, whose penultimate rule is already held by the project; adds only the correlates (pitch, intensity) and the focus-prosody findings. It neither narrows 'final or penultimate' to penultimate-dominant (Morgan does that) nor contradicts it. The statement held by the project for this work (reading 'unclear or contradictory', from the abstract only) can now be replaced by this body passage.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis makes no stress analysis of its own: it adopts Garvin's (1948c:37) statement that the phonological word ('contour') carries stress on the final or the penultimate syllable, treats each word as having one primary-stressed syllable, and names pitch and intensity as the correlates of word/phrase stress (after Morgan 1991:77). Its own contribution is sentence-level: focus is marked by higher mean pitch (probably a high pitch accent docking on the stressed syllable) and possibly intensity, not by duration or a dedicated position.
new_statements.exceptions: final-stressed contours are given as the alternative to penultimate (restating Garvin 1948c:37); no conditioning or list of exceptions is offered
new_statements.identity_note: Ktunaxa (Kutenai) as spoken by ʔaq̓am (St. Mary's band, Cranbrook BC) community members and other Ktunaxa Nation speakers in British Columbia recorded 2015-2016; the thesis uses the Ktunaxa community orthography; no dialect split is made for stress.
